Connectivity hooks::useOffline.summary: useOffline returns whether a Next.js app is currently offline. Enable experimental.useOffline to activate detection and automatic retries; otherwise, the hook always returns false.
Connectivity hooks::useOffline.explanation: Call useOffline in a Client Component to obtain a boolean connectivity state. Enable experimental.useOffline in next.config.ts to activate detection and automatic retries; without that setting, the hook remains false. It is false during server rendering and initial hydration, then reflects the browser’s state after mounting.
Connectivity hooks::useOffline.returns: A boolean: true when the app is offline; false when it is online or rendering on the server, including the initial value before hydration completes.

example.title: Show offline status
example.explanation: A Client Component reads the boolean and displays connectivity status.

useCases.title: Offline banner
useCases.scenario: Show an always-visible indicator when connectivity is lost.

useCases.title: Offline-aware loading UI
useCases.scenario: Tell users why a pending route or request has not completed.

useCases.title: Suspense fallback
useCases.scenario: Display a fallback while dynamic content waits for reconnection.

interview.question: What does useOffline return and what is it used for?
interview.answer: useOffline returns a boolean: true when the app is offline and false when it is online or rendering on the server. It is intended for connectivity-aware UI such as an offline banner or Suspense fallback.
interview.followUp: What happens before hydration? The hook returns false, and the first accurate value is obtained after the app mounts in the browser.

interview.question: How do you call useOffline?
interview.answer: The hook takes no parameters and is imported from next/offline. It must be called from a Client Component because it exposes browser connectivity state.
interview.followUp: How would you configure the feature? Set experimental.useOffline to true in next.config.ts, then restart the development or production server.

interview.question: What does enabling the configuration option change?
interview.answer: Enabling experimental.useOffline activates offline detection and automatic retry for blocked navigation, prefetch, and Server Action requests, while exposing the hook. When connectivity returns, blocked requests can complete automatically.
interview.followUp: What UI can show while a request waits? Use the boolean in a persistent banner or an offline-aware Suspense fallback.

keyPoints: The hook’s result is a boolean representing the app’s current offline state.
useOffline only reports status; the configuration option also enables detection and request retry behavior.
Import the hook from next/offline.
Call the hook without arguments.
The browser-provided state becomes accurate after client mounting.
A persistent connectivity banner is a supported use for the hook.
gotchas: The hook is experimental and may change, so it is not recommended for production use.
Forgetting experimental.useOffline makes the hook permanently report false.
Do not assume the initial false value proves the browser is online; it is also used before hydration finishes.

Connectivity hooks::useOffline and hydra.summary: useOffline exposes the app's offline state to Client Components as a boolean. Because server rendering and initial hydration return false, treat that initial value as progressive enhancement and rely on the post-mount value for accurate browser connectivity.
Connectivity hooks::useOffline and hydra.explanation: Enable experimental.useOffline, then call useOffline in a Client Component. The hook initially reports false during server rendering and hydration; after mounting, it reflects browser connectivity and failed supported requests, returning to false after connectivity is confirmed.
Connectivity hooks::useOffline and hydra.returns: A boolean: true when the app is offline; false when it is online or rendering on the server, including the initial value before hydration completes.

example.title: Show an offline banner
example.explanation: A Client Component reads the hook and displays feedback only while connectivity is unavailable.

useCases.title: Connectivity feedback
useCases.scenario: Show a persistent banner or status message when the user loses connectivity.

useCases.title: Offline loading state
useCases.scenario: Provide an offline-aware Suspense fallback while a supported request waits for reconnection.

useCases.title: Resilient navigation
useCases.scenario: Keep users informed during a prefetched soft navigation whose dynamic content is blocked by the network.

interview.question: What does useOffline return, and when is it true?
interview.answer: useOffline returns a boolean for Client Components. It is true when the browser is offline or a supported navigation, prefetch, or Server Action request fails; it returns false while online and during server rendering or initial hydration.
interview.followUp: Why can the first client-rendered value be misleading? Because server rendering and initial hydration deliberately use false; the browser-reported value becomes accurate after mount.

interview.question: How do you enable useOffline?
interview.answer: The experimental.useOffline configuration option must be enabled. That option activates connectivity detection and makes the hook available from next/offline; without it, the hook always returns false.
interview.followUp: What else does enabling the option do? It detects relevant network failures, polls while offline, and retries blocked requests after connectivity returns.

interview.question: What UI and navigation behavior does useOffline support?
interview.answer: The hook is useful for connectivity-aware UI such as an offline banner or an offline-aware Suspense fallback. A prefetched soft navigation can show its static shell while dynamic content waits, then the blocked request can complete when connectivity returns.
interview.followUp: Does it make every offline load work? No. A full reload still needs the browser to fetch HTML; complete offline loading requires a service worker.

keyPoints: Call useOffline() to obtain a boolean representing the app's current offline state.
The hook has no arguments and is called simply as useOffline().
False is the conservative initial value during server rendering and before hydration finishes.
After connectivity returns, blocked supported requests are retried and waiting dynamic content can stream in.
A persistent connectivity banner is a documented use for communicating offline state.
gotchas: The hook is inert unless experimental.useOffline is enabled; otherwise it always reports false.
The API is experimental and may change, so avoid treating it as a stable production contract.
Do not rely on the initial false value for immediate client-only connectivity decisions; wait until mounting.
Offline retry applies to supported soft navigations and requests, not a full reload that still needs HTML from the network.

Hook patterns::Active links from usePath.summary: Use usePathname in a small Client Component to compare the current route with each Link href. Import that component into a shared layout so active-link state updates without making the entire layout request-dependent.
Hook patterns::Active links from usePath.explanation: Extract navigation into a Client Component and call usePathname there. Compare the returned pathname with each Link destination to conditionally apply an active class; because the client component updates during navigation, a shared layout does not need to become request-dependent.
Hook patterns::Active links from usePath.returns: A string containing the current URL pathname.

example.title: Highlight the current navigation link
example.explanation: A small Client Component reads the current pathname and compares it with each link's href. Put this component inside a shared layout: the layout remains reusable, while the client-side navigation component re-renders as routes change.

useCases.title: Shared navigation
useCases.scenario: A site-wide header or sidebar needs to show which destination is selected.

useCases.title: Persistent route menus
useCases.scenario: A dashboard shell remains mounted while users move among nested routes.

useCases.title: Conditional link state
useCases.scenario: A link receives styling, an accessibility attribute, or an indicator only on its matching route.

interview.question: What does usePathname return?
interview.answer: usePathname is a Client Component hook that reads the current URL pathname. It takes no arguments and returns a string, excluding the query string.
interview.followUp: Why does this avoid making a shared layout request-dependent? Extracting the hook into a client navigation component lets the layout remain reusable while that component re-renders on navigation.

interview.question: How do you implement an active link?
interview.answer: Add 'use client' to the navigation component, import usePathname from next/navigation, then compare its result with each Link href. Apply the active class when the values match.
interview.followUp: How would you match a section rather than one exact route? Use a deliberate prefix or route-matching rule, taking care not to mark unrelated paths active.

interview.question: Why isolate navigation in a Client Component?
interview.answer: A shared layout can import a client navigation component that reads the pathname. Client Components re-render during navigation, so the navigation receives the latest pathname without requiring the whole layout to be request-dependent.
interview.followUp: What complication can rewrites introduce? The browser pathname may differ from the source pathname used during prerendering, which can affect initial active-state rendering.

keyPoints: Read the current pathname and use it as the comparison value for active-link logic.
Conditionally add a CSS class when the pathname equals the link destination.
The isolated navigation component updates after client-side route changes.
Keep the shared layout server-oriented by importing a dedicated client navigation component.
gotchas: The hook cannot be called directly in a Server Component; add 'use client' and isolate the navigation UI.

Hook patterns::Pending UI thresholds.summary: useLinkStatus exposes a Link navigation's pending state. Delay and initially hide its visual indicator so fast transitions do not flash.
Hook patterns::Pending UI thresholds.explanation: useLinkStatus exposes whether a Link navigation is still pending. Place a client component using the hook inside the Link, then combine the boolean with an initially invisible CSS animation that starts after a short delay; the hint appears only when navigation lasts beyond that threshold.
Hook patterns::Pending UI thresholds.returns: An object with one property: pending, a boolean that is true before history updates and false after.

example.title: Delayed navigation hint
example.explanation: The descendant observes the link's pending state, while CSS delays and initially hides the visual hint so quick navigations do not produce a flash.

useCases.title: Uncertain navigation start
useCases.scenario: Prefetching is disabled or incomplete and users need immediate local feedback.

useCases.title: Dynamic route feedback
useCases.scenario: A dynamic destination has no loading.js route fallback.

useCases.title: Flash-free pending UI
useCases.scenario: A link hint should appear only when a transition exceeds a short duration.

interview.question: What does useLinkStatus return and when is pending true?
interview.answer: It returns an object containing a pending boolean. The value is true before the browser history update and becomes false afterward.
interview.followUp: What should prevent a fast navigation indicator from flashing? Use an initial animation delay and begin with the indicator invisible, such as opacity: 0.

interview.question: How should the hook be placed in a component tree?
interview.answer: Render a client component that calls useLinkStatus as a descendant of the Link. The component can use pending to apply a class or otherwise show inline feedback.
interview.followUp: When is this hook especially useful? When prefetching is disabled or still in progress, or when a dynamic destination lacks loading.js.

interview.question: How can a pending hint avoid flashing during fast navigation?
interview.answer: A delayed animation acts as a threshold: quick transitions finish before the hint becomes visible, while slower transitions reveal it. The documentation gives 100ms as an example delay.
interview.followUp: What alternative should usually be preferred for route-wide loading? Use loading.js fallbacks and prefetching when they provide the desired experience.

keyPoints: Use the hook to drive small, link-local feedback while navigation is underway.
Disabling prefetch makes this localized pending signal more valuable because navigation may need visible feedback.
A threshold is needed because immediate indicators can briefly appear during transitions users would otherwise perceive as instant.
Delay the animation and start it transparent to suppress the hint until navigation exceeds the chosen threshold.
gotchas: Prefetched destinations can bypass the pending state, so the indicator may not appear.
Rapid clicks are tracked only for the most recently selected link.
Do not call the hook from an unrelated component outside the Link subtree.

Hook patterns::Search params are read-on.summary: useSearchParams exposes the current query string through a read-only URLSearchParams interface. To change parameters, copy them into a new URLSearchParams object, modify the copy, and navigate with the new query string.
Hook patterns::Search params are read-on.explanation: useSearchParams provides the current URL query string through a read-only URLSearchParams interface. To change a value, serialize it into a new URLSearchParams instance, apply the mutation there, and navigate with useRouter or another supported navigation API.
Hook patterns::Search params are read-on.returns: A read-only URLSearchParams interface for reading the URL query string.

example.title: Update a query parameter safely
example.explanation: Copy the current values into a new URLSearchParams object, modify that copy, and navigate with the resulting query string.

useCases.title: Read client-side filters
useCases.scenario: A client-side search field needs to initialize from or react to a query value such as search.

useCases.title: Update URL state
useCases.scenario: A sorting or filtering control must preserve existing parameters while changing one value.

useCases.title: Handle multi-value parameters
useCases.scenario: A component needs to inspect repeated query-key values.

interview.question: What does useSearchParams return, and how do you update a value?
interview.answer: useSearchParams is a Client Component hook that reads the current URL query string. Its returned URLSearchParams interface is read-only, so changes require copying its serialized value into a new URLSearchParams object and navigating with the updated string.
interview.followUp: How would a Server Component read query parameters? Use the corresponding Page's searchParams prop instead, because this hook is not supported in Server Components.

interview.question: What is the hook's signature and what operations does its result support?
interview.answer: The hook takes no parameters. It returns a read-only URLSearchParams interface whose reading utilities include get, getAll, has, keys, values, entries, and toString.
interview.followUp: What should a component do when it needs to preserve repeated values? Use getAll rather than get, because get returns only the first associated value.

interview.question: Show the safe pattern for changing one query parameter.
interview.answer: First create a new URLSearchParams from searchParams.toString(), then change the new instance and pass its serialized result to router.push or another navigation method. This preserves the current query values while changing only the intended parameter.
interview.followUp: Why can reading query parameters in a layout be problematic? Layouts do not rerender on navigation, so their values could become stale; read them in a Page or Client Component instead.

keyPoints: Use the hook in a Client Component when UI logic needs to inspect the current URL query string.
The returned object is for reading, not mutation; edits must happen on a separately constructed URLSearchParams object.
Invoke the hook without arguments: useSearchParams().
Use get for a single value; when a key can repeat, select getAll to retrieve every value.
gotchas: Call this hook only from a Client Component; Server Components should use the page searchParams prop when they need query parameters.
Do not attempt to call set, delete, or append on the returned object; create a separate URLSearchParams instance first.

Hook patterns::Segment hooks at the root.summary: useSelectedLayoutSegment reads the active route segment immediately below the layout where a Client Component calls it. In a root layout, use null as the fallback for the root route, then map child segment names to navigation state.
Hook patterns::Segment hooks at the root.explanation: Call this Client Component hook from a component under a layout to inspect the active segment immediately below that layout. At the root layout, it identifies the first matched child segment; when the current route is the root itself, it returns null, so navigation UI should define an explicit fallback state.

parameters.name: parallelRouteKey
parameters.description: Optional parallel route key used to read the active segment within a named slot.

Hook patterns::Segment hooks at the root.returns: A string containing the active segment one level below the calling layout, or null when no such segment exists.

example.title: Root navigation with a fallback
example.explanation: In a client component rendered by the root layout, the hook reads the first active route segment below that layout. Since the root route has no child segment, null is returned there, so the example maps null to the Home state.

useCases.title: Active root navigation
useCases.scenario: A root navigation bar needs to mark the first-level route as active.

useCases.title: Layout-local tabs
useCases.scenario: Tabs inside a parent layout correspond to its immediate child routes.

useCases.title: Parallel-route slot state
useCases.scenario: A layout renders a named parallel slot and needs that slot's current child.

interview.question: What does useSelectedLayoutSegment return in a root layout?
interview.answer: It returns the active route segment one level below the layout where the hook runs. In a root layout, that means the first matched child segment; on the root route itself, the result is null.
interview.followUp: How would you read every active segment? Use useSelectedLayoutSegments, which returns an array of active segments below the calling layout.

interview.question: Where can this hook be called?
interview.answer: The component calling it must be a Client Component, and the hook is imported from next/navigation. Add the 'use client' directive to that component before using the hook.
interview.followUp: What if a parallel route slot is the target? Pass that slot's parallel route key as the optional argument.

interview.question: What is the optional argument used for?
interview.answer: The optional parameter is a parallel route key. Supplying it makes the hook read the active segment within that named slot instead of the default route tree.
interview.followUp: Do slots change the URL path? No: slots are not route segments and do not affect URL structure.

keyPoints: The hook observes only the child segment immediately below the calling layout.
Use it to style tabs or links in a parent layout according to the active child route.
Its signature accepts an optional string identifying a parallel route slot.
The result is either the active segment name or null when no child segment matches.
Choose useSelectedLayoutSegments when navigation logic needs the full descendant segment list.
gotchas: The hook can only be used from a Client Component, so add 'use client' to the component that calls it.
It does not report every segment in a deeply nested URL; use the plural hook when the complete active path is needed.
The root route has no child segment, so handle null rather than assuming the return value is always a string.
A catch-all match is returned as one joined string, not as separate segment values.

Hook patterns::Typed useParams.summary: Typed useParams reads dynamic URL segments through a typed parameter object in an App Router Client Component. Describe the segment names and value shapes with the hook's generic instead of casting the returned record.
Hook patterns::Typed useParams.explanation: In an App Router Client Component, call useParams with a type describing the route's dynamic segments. The hook returns the current URL values under those property names, allowing TypeScript to check reads without casting the returned record.

parameters.name: T
parameters.description: Optional generic describing the dynamic-parameter object and its segment value types.

Hook patterns::Typed useParams.returns: An object containing the current route's filled-in dynamic parameters.

example.title: Read typed dynamic segments
example.explanation: A Client Component supplies the generated route shape as the hook's generic, so each dynamic segment is accessed with a named string property.

useCases.title: Render nested dynamic segments
useCases.scenario: A product page uses a `[category]` and `[product]` route and needs both values for its UI.

useCases.title: Handle catch-all paths
useCases.scenario: A route uses `[...slug]` and needs the matched path pieces as an array.

useCases.title: Keep route reads type-safe
useCases.scenario: A shared Client Component receives a route-specific parameter shape and should preserve property-level type checking.

interview.question: What does useParams do?
interview.answer: useParams is a Client Component hook from next/navigation. It reads dynamic parameters filled in by the current URL and returns them as an object.
interview.followUp: How should the object be typed? Use a generic describing the route's segment names and value shapes, then read those named properties.

interview.question: How do you type the returned params?
interview.answer: The generic should model each dynamic segment as a property, such as `{ slug: string }` for a `[slug]` segment. This gives the returned object named, typed fields instead of requiring a cast at each use.
interview.followUp: What determines whether a value is a string or an array? The route convention: catch-all segments produce arrays, while ordinary dynamic segments produce strings.

interview.question: Why avoid casting the returned record?
interview.answer: The current route determines which dynamic parameters are filled, and the hook exposes them through the returned record. The route's segment convention determines the corresponding parameter shape.
interview.followUp: What should be checked when a parameter may be absent? Model optional catch-all segments as optional array properties rather than assuming a string is always present.

keyPoints: Import useParams from next/navigation and call it inside a Client Component.
The values come from the dynamic segments matched by the current URL.
Access values as properties on the returned object.
gotchas: useParams must run in a Client Component; it is not a Server Component API.

Hook patterns::useRouter in event handle.summary: Call useRouter at the top level of an App Router Client Component, then use the returned router inside an event handler. Use methods such as push for imperative client-side navigation.
Hook patterns::useRouter in event handle.explanation: In an App Router Client Component, import useRouter from next/navigation and call it at the component's top level. Keep the returned router available to an event handler, then invoke a navigation method such as push when the event occurs; do not call the Hook inside the handler.

parameters.name: href, options
parameters.description: Destination route and optional scroll and transition settings supplied to a router navigation method.

Hook patterns::useRouter in event handle.returns: A router object with push, replace, refresh, prefetch, back, and forward navigation methods.

example.title: Navigate from a click handler
example.explanation: The Client Component obtains the router once at render time, then the click handler uses its push method to navigate.

useCases.title: Post-action navigation
useCases.scenario: A button submits a form and then moves the user to a result or confirmation route.

useCases.title: Conditional navigation
useCases.scenario: An interaction chooses a destination dynamically rather than rendering a fixed link.

useCases.title: History controls
useCases.scenario: A control must move backward or forward through browser history.

interview.question: How should useRouter be used in an event handler?
interview.answer: useRouter is a Client Component Hook for programmatic route changes. Call it at the component level, then invoke router.push from the event handler.
interview.followUp: What should be used for ordinary navigational links? Prefer the Link component unless imperative navigation is specifically needed.

interview.question: Which import and navigation method are correct in the App Router?
interview.answer: Import useRouter from next/navigation, not next/router. The hook returns a router object whose push method performs client-side navigation and adds a history entry.
interview.followUp: How would you replace the current history entry? Use router.replace with the destination instead of router.push.

interview.question: What is the event-handler alternative to redirect?
interview.answer: redirect is not for event handlers in Client Components. For a click or other event, use the router returned by useRouter and call push with the target route.
interview.followUp: How can route changes be observed in the App Router? Compose Client Component hooks such as usePathname and useSearchParams.

keyPoints: useRouter enables imperative navigation from Client Components.
Use the App Router's next/navigation import.
router.push navigates to a route on the client and can receive navigation options.
push preserves the previous location by adding a browser-history entry.
back returns to the preceding browser-history location.
forward moves to the next available browser-history location.
gotchas: Use the App Router import path; next/router is the wrong API for this pattern.
Do not use redirect in a client-side event handler; use the router's push method instead.
Prefer Link for ordinary navigation, reserving useRouter for cases that require imperative control.

Hook patterns::useServerInsertedHTML.summary: useServerInsertedHTML lets a Client Component insert collected CSS-in-JS styles into server-rendered HTML. Use it with a style registry so styles are emitted before content that needs them.
Hook patterns::useServerInsertedHTML.explanation: In a Client Component, create a style registry for the render and register a callback with useServerInsertedHTML. The callback returns the collected style elements so Next.js places them before rendered content that depends on those rules, then flushes the registry to prevent reuse of already inserted styles.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: A callback that produces the React content to insert into the server-rendered HTML.

Hook patterns::useServerInsertedHTML.returns: The page documents the hook's callback-based usage but does not state a separate return value for the hook.

example.title: Style registry for styled-jsx
example.explanation: Creates a client-side style registry, inserts its collected styles during server rendering, then clears the registry.

useCases.title: Collect and emit generated styles
useCases.scenario: A CSS-in-JS library generates styles while the App Router performs the initial server render.

useCases.title: Keep styles ahead of dependent markup
useCases.scenario: Streaming HTML may reach the browser before all component output is complete.

useCases.title: Wrap the application with a style registry
useCases.scenario: A provider must supply a registry to styled-jsx or another compatible CSS-in-JS integration.

interview.question: How is useServerInsertedHTML used with CSS-in-JS?
interview.answer: It registers a server-insertion callback that returns markup during server rendering. In the CSS-in-JS pattern, that callback reads the registry's collected styles, returns them, and then flushes the registry.
interview.followUp: Why flush after reading the styles? Flushing clears the collected rules so the same styles are not inserted repeatedly during the render.

interview.question: What pieces are required for this integration?
interview.answer: The documented pattern uses three parts: a registry that collects rules, useServerInsertedHTML to inject them, and a Client Component wrapping the application during initial server-side rendering.
interview.followUp: What ordering requirement matters? Insert the rules before content that may use them, so the generated HTML has the styles in place first.

interview.question: Why does the example place the hook in a client provider?
interview.answer: The hook is used from a Client Component that owns the style registry. The component wraps the application and supplies the registry to the CSS-in-JS library while the server performs the initial render.
interview.followUp: Can any CSS-in-JS library use this automatically? No; the library must provide a way to collect generated rules and return them as renderable style output.

keyPoints: Pair the hook with a registry that gathers every CSS rule produced during the render.
Use the hook to place collected rules ahead of content that depends on those rules.
Put the registry in a Client Component that wraps the app for the initial server render.
Read the registry's generated style elements inside the insertion callback.
gotchas: When using styled-jsx in a Client Component, use styled-jsx version 5.1.0 or later.
The registry is global during server rendering, and collected styles are extracted and flushed into the document head.
The callback should insert the rules before dependent content so styling is available in the right order.

Layout hooks::Segment-aware navigation.summary: Read active route segments beneath a layout to build segment-aware navigation, breadcrumbs, or tabs. Use the singular hook for one immediate child, the plural hook for multiple segments, and an optional key for a parallel slot.
Layout hooks::Segment-aware navigation.explanation: Place this Client Component in a layout when navigation needs to know which immediate child route is active. The singular hook returns one segment or null; the plural hook returns all active segments below the calling layout. Passing a parallel-route key reads the segment belonging to that named slot, while route-group names may appear in the plural result.

parameters.name: parallelRouteKey
parameters.description: Optional name of the parallel-route slot whose active segment should be read.

Layout hooks::Segment-aware navigation.returns: useSelectedLayoutSegment returns the active segment as a string or null. useSelectedLayoutSegments returns an array of active segment strings, or an empty array when none exist.

example.title: Highlight the active child route
example.explanation: A Client Component reads the active child segment and marks the matching navigation link as current.

useCases.title: Active tabs
useCases.scenario: A parent layout highlights the currently selected child tab.

useCases.title: Breadcrumbs
useCases.scenario: A layout builds navigation context from several descendant segments.

useCases.title: Parallel-slot navigation
useCases.scenario: A named slot has its own tabs or navigation state.

interview.question: What does useSelectedLayoutSegment return?
interview.answer: The singular hook reads the active route segment one level below the layout where it runs and returns a string or null. It is suited to tabs or other navigation whose state depends on one immediate child.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect deeper descendants? Use useSelectedLayoutSegments, which returns the active segments below the calling layout as an array.

interview.question: When would you choose the plural hook?
interview.answer: useSelectedLayoutSegments returns an array of active segments one level down from the layout context, or an empty array when there are none. It is useful when UI such as breadcrumbs needs multiple selected segments.
interview.followUp: What can make those values unsuitable for direct display? Route Groups are included, so filter them if they should not appear in the UI.

interview.question: How do these hooks work with parallel routes?
interview.answer: Both hooks accept an optional parallelRouteKey. That key selects the active segment inside a named parallel-route slot rather than the default route branch.
interview.followUp: Why might a tab layout use this? A layout inside a slot can let users navigate that slot independently, which is useful for tabs.

keyPoints: Use the singular hook for the immediate child segment beneath the layout containing the Client Component.
It can drive active styling for tabs or similar navigation rendered by a parent layout.
Use the plural hook when the navigation needs the descendant segment path rather than only its first segment.
The plural result is an array of strings representing active segments relative to the calling layout.
Supply a named parallel-route key to read the active segment from that slot.
The plural hook also supports selecting the active segment within a parallel-route slot.
gotchas: Filter route-group names before displaying plural-hook results when those grouping names should not appear in breadcrumbs or navigation.
Handle the plural hook's empty-array result when the current layout has no active descendant.

Layout hooks::useSelectedLayoutSegment.summary: A Client Component hook that reads the active route segment immediately below the layout containing it. Use it for layout navigation state, optionally targeting a parallel-route slot.
Layout hooks::useSelectedLayoutSegment.explanation: Call this Client Component hook from a layout to inspect the currently selected child route segment. It examines only the next segment below that layout, returns the segment name when present, and returns null when no child segment exists. Pass a parallel route key when the segment should come from a particular slot.

parameters.name: parallelRouteKey
parameters.description: Optional name of the parallel route slot whose active child segment should be read.

Layout hooks::useSelectedLayoutSegment.returns: A string containing the active segment, or null when no such segment exists.

example.title: Highlight an active child route
example.explanation: This client navigation link compares its target with the child segment directly below the layout that renders it, then applies an active class.

useCases.title: Mark the current tab active
useCases.scenario: A parent layout contains tabs for child routes such as overview and settings.

useCases.title: Inspect a slot's selected child
useCases.scenario: A layout renders navigation for a named parallel route.

useCases.title: Drive child-link styling
useCases.scenario: A shared navigation component needs route-relative state without parsing the full pathname.

interview.question: What does useSelectedLayoutSegment return?
interview.answer: It is a Client Component hook imported from next/navigation. It reads the active route segment one level below the layout where it runs and returns that segment or null.
interview.followUp: How would you read every active descendant segment? Use useSelectedLayoutSegments, which returns an array rather than a single segment.

interview.question: What is the optional parameter used for?
interview.answer: The optional argument is parallelRouteKey. It selects the active segment within a named parallel-route slot instead of the default route.
interview.followUp: Why might a slot-specific value differ from the URL's apparent main segment? Parallel routes maintain independent route branches, so the selected slot can have its own active segment.

interview.question: Give a practical use for this hook and identify its component constraint.
interview.answer: The hook is intended for layout-level navigation UI, such as tabs or links whose styling depends on the active child route. It must run in a Client Component.
interview.followUp: What should be considered when cacheComponents is enabled? Add a Suspense boundary if the segment cannot be determined during prerendering.

The returned segment is relative to the containing layout, not necessarily the first segment of the full URL.
Use it to derive active styling for tabs or links controlled by child routes.
Provide a slot key to inspect the active segment in a parallel route.
Expect a string for an active child or null when the layout has no selected child segment.
gotchas: It does not provide the complete active path; use useSelectedLayoutSegments when all descendant segments are needed.
A catch-all match is exposed as one joined string rather than as separate segment values.

interview.question: What does useSelectedLayoutSegment return, and why is it useful for tabs?
interview.answer: It is a Client Component hook imported from next/navigation. When called from a layout, it returns the active route segment immediately below that layout, making it suitable for comparing against tab identifiers.
interview.followUp: How would you support tabs in a parallel route? Pass that slot's parallelRouteKey to the hook so it reads the active segment within the slot.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the optional argument?
interview.answer: The optional argument is parallelRouteKey. Supplying it selects the parallel-route slot whose active child segment should be read instead of using the default route.
interview.followUp: What is the key distinction between a slot and a route segment? A named slot is created with the @folder convention, but slots do not change the URL structure.

interview.question: What are the important return-value edge cases?
interview.answer: It returns a string containing the active segment, or null when no segment exists at that layout level. A catch-all route is represented as one string containing its matched path segments joined together.
interview.followUp: What should be used when all active descendants are needed? useSelectedLayoutSegments returns the active segments below the layout as an array.

keyPoints: Use it inside a Client Component to inspect the child route directly beneath the layout that invokes it.
A tab bar can compare each tab's segment name with the hook result to choose the active styling.
Pass a parallel-route key when the tab state belongs to a named slot rather than the default route.
Treat null as the no-active-child case, such as when the layout route itself is being displayed.
Choose the plural hook when the UI must inspect multiple descendant segments instead of only the immediate child.
gotchas: It does not provide every descendant segment; use useSelectedLayoutSegments when navigation needs the full set.
For routes whose active segment is unavailable during prerendering, wrap the component or an ancestor in Suspense.
A catch-all child does not return one segment per path component; its matched path is returned as one joined string.

It returns the segments as an ordered string array, optionally reading from a named parallel-route slot; when no child segment is active, the array is empty.

parameters.name: parallelRouteKey
parameters.description: Optional parallel-route slot key. When supplied, the hook reads the active route segment within that slot.

Layout hooks::useSelectedLayoutSegments.returns: An array of strings representing the active segments one level below the calling layout, or an empty array when none exist.

example.title: Render active child segments
example.explanation: This Client Component renders each active segment beneath the layout as a breadcrumb item.

useCases.scenario: A parent layout needs to show the current nested path as a breadcrumb trail.

useCases.title: Section navigation
useCases.scenario: A layout renders navigation whose sections depend on the active nested route.

useCases.title: Parallel-route navigation
useCases.scenario: A layout needs route state from a named slot such as an auth or dashboard parallel route.

interview.question: What does `useSelectedLayoutSegments` return?
interview.answer: It is a Client Component hook that reads active route segments below the layout calling it. The result is an array of strings, making it suitable for breadcrumbs and other parent-layout navigation.
interview.followUp: How do you read a segment from a parallel route? Pass that slot's key as the optional `parallelRouteKey` argument.

interview.question: What is the hook's signature and purpose of its optional argument?
interview.answer: Its signature is `useSelectedLayoutSegments(parallelRouteKey?: string)`. Omitting the argument reads the default route; supplying a key reads the active segment within that parallel-route slot.
interview.followUp: What happens when the slot has no active segment? The hook returns an empty array.

interview.question: When is Suspense needed with this hook?
interview.answer: The hook can resolve during prerendering when the active segments are known, so no Suspense boundary is needed in that case. If an uncovered dynamic parameter is not known until the request, the hook suspends and requires Suspense.
interview.followUp: Why does the build fail without Suspense in that case? There is no fallback available for the prerendered shell.

keyPoints: Use it in a layout to inspect active child route segments.
Typical applications include breadcrumbs and section navigation.
The optional argument selects a parallel-route slot.
No active child segment produces an empty array.
Known active segments can be obtained during prerendering without Suspense.
gotchas: The hook must be used in a Client Component.
The result is scoped to the layout where the hook runs, rather than representing the entire URL.
For dynamic parameters not covered by `generateStaticParams`, place the component or a parent inside Suspense.

It returns the segments one level down as an array, includes route-group names, and can target a parallel-route slot with an optional key; filter group entries before using the result in visible navigation UI.

parameters.name: parallelRouteKey
parameters.description: Optional key identifying the parallel-route slot whose active segment should be read.

example.title: Filter route groups from breadcrumbs
example.explanation: Reads active child segments and removes route-group entries before displaying them.

useCases.title: Section labels

useCases.scenario: A layout renders navigation for a named parallel slot.

interview.question: What does useSelectedLayoutSegments return?
interview.answer: It is a Client Component hook that reads active route segments below the layout where it is called. The result is an array of strings, or an empty array when no child segments exist.
interview.followUp: How would you read a segment from a parallel route? Pass that slot's parallelRouteKey as the optional argument.

interview.question: How should route groups be handled when building breadcrumbs?
interview.answer: Route groups are part of the returned segments even though they are usually implementation details for UI. Remove entries that begin with the route-group marker before rendering them.
interview.followUp: Why should breadcrumbs avoid displaying them? Route groups organize layouts without representing user-facing URL path segments.

interview.question: How can the hook inspect a parallel route?
interview.answer: The hook accepts an optional parallelRouteKey. Supplying it reads the active route segment within that parallel-route slot rather than the default route.
interview.followUp: What happens for an unresolved dynamic parameter during prerendering? The hook suspends, so wrap the component or an ancestor in Suspense.

keyPoints: Use it in a Client Component to inspect active segments beneath the calling layout.
The returned array contains the active child segments one level below the layout.
If the layout has no active child segment, the hook returns an empty array.
Filter entries beginning with a bracket to hide route-group segments from rendered UI.
An optional parallel-route key lets the hook read the active segment inside a specific slot.
gotchas: Route groups are included in the returned array, so filter them before showing breadcrumbs or labels.
With dynamic parameters not covered by generateStaticParams, provide a Suspense boundary because the hook may suspend during prerendering.

Navigation hooks::router.push.summary: Programmatically navigate to a route from a Client Component while adding a new browser-history entry. Use the optional options object to control scrolling and transition types.
Navigation hooks::router.push.explanation: In a Client Component, obtain the router with useRouter from next/navigation and call push with the destination string. Next.js performs client-side navigation, records the destination as a new browser-history entry, and normally scrolls to the top; pass scroll: false to preserve the current scroll position.
Navigation hooks::router.push.syntax: router.push(href: string, { scroll: boolean, transitionTypes: string[] })

parameters.name: href
parameters.description: Destination route to navigate to.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings; scroll controls scroll restoration and transitionTypes supplies transition labels.

Navigation hooks::router.push.returns: Performs client-side navigation; the documentation does not specify a return value.

example.title: Navigate from a button
example.explanation: A client component calls push in an event handler to navigate to the dashboard while creating a history entry.

useCases.title: Navigate after an event
useCases.scenario: A button submits a form and then opens the newly created record.

useCases.title: Update client-driven URL state
useCases.scenario: A filter updates the URL query string without a full page reload.

useCases.title: Advance through a flow
useCases.scenario: A workflow step moves the user to the next route while preserving browser back navigation.

interview.question: What does router.push do in the App Router?
interview.answer: Use useRouter from next/navigation inside a Client Component, then call router.push('/target') in an event handler. It performs client-side navigation and adds a new browser-history entry.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid changing the scroll position? Pass the options object with scroll: false, for example router.push('/target', { scroll: false }).

interview.question: What arguments does router.push accept?
interview.answer: The first argument is the destination href string. The optional options object supports scroll, and the current API also supports transitionTypes for the navigation transition.
interview.followUp: What happens to history if replacement rather than addition is required? Use router.replace, which navigates without adding a new browser-history entry.

interview.question: When is router.push appropriate?
interview.answer: It is intended for programmatic navigation, such as a button or another event handler in a Client Component. For declarative navigation, Next.js also provides the Link component.
interview.followUp: When should an event-handler redirect use the hook rather than redirect? The documentation recommends the useRouter push method for redirects initiated from Client Component event handlers.

keyPoints: Use the hook when navigation must be triggered by component logic rather than a declarative link.
Its signature takes a destination string and an optional navigation-options object.
The route changes through client-side navigation instead of requiring a full document reload.
Back-button behavior can return to the page that preceded the push.
Set scroll to false when navigation should retain the current scroll position.
Transition type values can be forwarded to React's transition API during navigation.
gotchas: Validate or construct destinations from trusted data; unsafe URLs can create an XSS vulnerability.
The App Router API uses next/navigation; importing the Pages Router version is incorrect here.

Navigation hooks::router.refresh.summary: router.refresh() requests a fresh server render of the current route, refetching route data and re-rendering Server Components. It merges the result while preserving unaffected client state and browser position.
Navigation hooks::router.refresh.explanation: Calling router.refresh() requests the current route again, fetches server data, and re-renders its Server Components. Next.js reconciles the resulting React Server Component payload into the existing UI, preserving unaffected client state and browser position; cached server data may still produce the same result.

example.title: Refresh the current route
example.explanation: A client component button requests a new server render for the current route while retaining unaffected client state and scroll position.

useCases.title: Reflect a completed mutation
useCases.scenario: A user submits or completes an operation and the current route should display its latest server-rendered values.

useCases.title: Re-evaluate request-time data
useCases.scenario: The response depends on request-time cookies or headers and the current UI should be rerun without navigation.

useCases.title: Refresh in place
useCases.scenario: A route's server-rendered content needs a manual client-triggered rerender while local component state and scroll should remain.

interview.question: What does router.refresh() do?
interview.answer: router.refresh() makes a new request for the current route, refetches data, and re-renders Server Components. The updated React Server Component payload is merged into the client without discarding unaffected React or browser state.
interview.followUp: How would you make cached server data change as well? Use revalidatePath or revalidateTag to invalidate the relevant server-side cache before or instead of relying on the client refresh.

interview.question: What state is preserved by router.refresh()?
interview.answer: It preserves unaffected client-side React state, such as useState, and browser state, such as scroll position. It refreshes the current route rather than navigating to a different URL.
interview.followUp: What cache does it clear? It clears the Client Cache for the current route, but leaves server-side cached data intact.

interview.question: Why might router.refresh() appear not to update data?
interview.answer: A refresh can return the same result when the route's fetch requests are cached. To obtain changed server data, invalidate the applicable server-side cache with revalidatePath or revalidateTag.
interview.followUp: When is router.refresh() still useful without invalidation? It can rerun the route request and reconcile the UI while preserving client and browser state, especially when the response depends on request-time values.

keyPoints: The method targets the currently displayed route; it does not require a destination URL.
It initiates a server request, repeats data requests, and renders the route's Server Components again.
The new server-rendered payload is merged into the existing client UI rather than replacing unaffected client state.
Browser position, including scroll position, remains intact through the refresh.
The current route's Client Cache is cleared as part of the operation.
Request-time values such as cookies and headers can cause the refreshed response to differ.
gotchas: A refresh does not guarantee newer data when the underlying fetch requests remain cached.
router.refresh() does not invalidate server-side cached data; use a server-cache invalidation API when that is required.

Navigation hooks::router.replace.summary: `router.replace` performs client-side navigation to a route without adding a new browser-history entry. Use it when the current URL should be replaced rather than retained for Back navigation.
Navigation hooks::router.replace.explanation: Call `useRouter()` in a Client Component and invoke `router.replace` with the destination string. Next.js performs client-side navigation without creating another browser-history entry; the optional scroll setting controls whether navigation scrolls to the top.
Navigation hooks::router.replace.syntax: router.replace(href: string, { scroll: boolean, transitionTypes: string[] })

parameters.name: href
parameters.description: Route or URL to navigate to.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional navigation settings, including `scroll` and `transitionTypes`.

Navigation hooks::router.replace.returns: Performs client-side navigation to the supplied route without adding a browser-history entry; the method returns no documented value.

example.title: Replace the current route with a search URL
example.explanation: Submits a search while replacing the current history entry, so repeated searches do not create back-button entries.

useCases.title: Update query parameters as users submit or change filters without creating a Back-button entry for every change.
useCases.scenario: Search and filtering

useCases.title: Replace a temporary or obsolete route after completing an action so users do not return to it with Back.
useCases.scenario: Redirect after an intermediate step

useCases.title: Normalize a destination's path or query representation while keeping the current history position.
useCases.scenario: Canonicalizing a URL

interview.question: What does `router.replace` do?
interview.answer: `router.replace` performs client-side navigation to the supplied route without adding a new entry to the browser history. It is useful when the current URL should be superseded rather than preserved for Back navigation.
interview.followUp: How can scrolling be controlled? Pass `{ scroll: false }` as the second argument when navigation should not scroll to the top.

interview.question: How is `router.replace` used in the App Router?
interview.answer: Import `useRouter` from `next/navigation`, call it inside a Client Component, and invoke `router.replace(href)`. The method accepts a destination string and an optional options object.
interview.followUp: What must be checked before passing a dynamic destination? Ensure the URL is trusted and sanitized, because unsanitized values can introduce XSS.

interview.question: How does replacement affect browser history?
interview.answer: Replacing a route updates the URL through client-side navigation while discarding the current browser-history position as a separate entry. Consequently, the previous state is not available through the browser Back action.
interview.followUp: When should a different hook be used for URL data? Use `usePathname` for the current pathname and `useSearchParams` for query parameters; `useRouter` does not provide those values.

keyPoints: The destination replaces the current history position instead of creating another Back-button step.
Use the hook when navigation must be triggered by component logic, such as a submit handler or button event.
Its signature takes a destination string and an options object for scroll behavior and transition types.
Set `scroll: false` when replacement should preserve the current scroll position.
gotchas: Validate or construct destination URLs from trusted, controlled values; unsafe input can create an XSS vulnerability.

Navigation hooks::useLinkStatus.summary: Track an individual Link's pending navigation state and show localized feedback while navigation completes. Use it for subtle indicators such as shimmers, especially when prefetching is unavailable or delayed.
Navigation hooks::useLinkStatus.explanation: useLinkStatus provides localized feedback for a Link transition. A descendant client component reads its pending boolean and can render a shimmer or other subtle indicator until the navigation progresses past the pending phase.
Navigation hooks::useLinkStatus.returns: An object with one property, pending: boolean. pending is true before history updates and false after.

example.title: Inline navigation indicator
example.explanation: Place the client component that calls the hook inside a Link. It reads pending and applies temporary feedback while navigation is still underway.

useCases.title: Indicate delayed dynamic navigation
useCases.scenario: The destination is dynamic and has no loading.js route fallback.

useCases.title: Show feedback with disabled prefetching
useCases.scenario: A Link uses prefetch={false}, so navigation work begins after the click.

useCases.title: Render inline transition feedback
useCases.scenario: A clicked link needs a small visual cue rather than a page-wide loading UI.

interview.question: What does useLinkStatus return?
interview.answer: It is a hook for observing a Link's pending navigation state. It returns an object whose pending property is true before history updates and false afterward.
interview.followUp: Where must the consuming component be placed? It must be a descendant of the Link whose navigation it should observe.

interview.question: What is the hook's signature?
interview.answer: The hook takes no arguments. Call it as useLinkStatus() and destructure the returned pending boolean.
interview.followUp: What should replace it for route-wide loading UI? Prefer a route-level loading.js fallback when that broader behavior is appropriate.

interview.question: When is useLinkStatus useful?
interview.answer: It is most useful when Link prefetching is disabled or still in progress, or when a dynamic destination lacks loading.js. It supplies localized visual feedback while navigation completes.
interview.followUp: When might no pending phase appear despite a click? A prefetched route, a static production destination, or a route with loading.js can make the transition effectively immediate.

keyPoints: It exposes whether an individual Link navigation is currently pending.
Its intended UI is localized feedback such as a shimmer or indicator near the clicked link.
A useful scenario is a Link with disabled or unfinished prefetching, where navigation may be delayed.
Dynamic routes without a loading.js fallback are another situation where the hook can improve perceived responsiveness.
The return shape is an object containing only the pending field.
pending changes from true before the history update to false after it.
gotchas: The hook only works in a component descended from the relevant Link.
Do not assume pending becomes true when the destination was already prefetched.
Rapid clicks replace earlier feedback with the last clicked link's state.
Use this API only with App Router navigation.

Navigation hooks::useLinkStatus pending.summary: useLinkStatus tracks a Link's pending navigation state. Put a Client Component descendant inside the Link to show a small inline indicator without replacing shared navigation UI.
Navigation hooks::useLinkStatus pending.explanation: useLinkStatus exposes whether its containing Link is waiting for navigation. Render a descendant Client Component inside the Link and use the boolean to add a subtle inline indicator; route-level loading.js remains preferable for broader loading UI.
Navigation hooks::useLinkStatus pending.returns: An object with one property: pending (boolean), true before history updates and false after.

example.title: Inline pending indicator
example.explanation: A Client Component nested inside a Link reads that link's pending state and adds a local visual class while navigation is underway. The Link and its surrounding UI remain mounted, so only the small indicator changes.

useCases.title: Show a local shimmer
useCases.scenario: A destination has prefetch={false} and needs immediate click feedback.

useCases.title: Signal dynamic-route loading
useCases.scenario: A dynamic route lacks loading.js and navigation may take noticeable time.

useCases.title: Preserve navigation context
useCases.scenario: A shared nav shell should stay mounted while only the clicked Link changes appearance.

interview.question: What does useLinkStatus return, and when is pending true?
interview.answer: useLinkStatus is a Client Component hook that returns an object containing pending. The value is true before history updates and false after navigation completes.
interview.followUp: How can a developer make the pending phase more likely to appear? Set prefetch={false} on the Link, while remembering that route-level loading.js may still be the better fallback.

interview.question: Where must the hook be used?
interview.answer: The hook must run in a descendant of the Link whose navigation it represents. This lets a small child indicator respond without replacing the shared navigation shell.
interview.followUp: What happens if the component is outside Link? It cannot observe that Link's pending state, so the component must be moved into the Link subtree.

interview.question: When is useLinkStatus most useful?
interview.answer: It is useful when prefetching is disabled or still in progress, and for dynamic destinations without loading.js. If the route has already been prefetched, the pending state can be skipped.
interview.followUp: When should inline feedback be avoided? If navigation is normally instant or loading.js already provides an immediate route-level fallback, the extra indicator may add little value.

keyPoints: It reports whether a particular Link's navigation is currently pending.
Its intended role is localized feedback such as a shimmer, not replacement of the whole navigation shell.
Disabling Link prefetching is a practical situation where this indicator provides visible feedback.
The hook's result is an object whose only documented field is pending.
The pending flag turns on before the browser history update and turns off afterward.
Use loading.js for route-wide fallback UI and prefetching when the goal is instant navigation.
gotchas: Call the hook only from a component rendered inside the associated Link.
A prefetched destination can navigate without exposing a pending phase.
Rapidly clicking different links does not keep every link marked pending.
Use this hook with App Router navigation, not the Pages Router.

Navigation hooks::useRouter.summary: useRouter enables imperative navigation from Next.js App Router Client Components. It can change or replace history, refresh the current route, prefetch a destination, and traverse browser history.
Navigation hooks::useRouter.explanation: Import useRouter from next/navigation inside a Client Component, then call methods on the returned router object. push and replace perform client-side navigation, refresh re-requests and re-renders the current route while preserving unaffected client and browser state, back and forward traverse browser history, and prefetch prepares a route for faster navigation.

parameters.name: href
parameters.description: Destination URL for push, replace, and prefetch; scroll and transitionTypes are optional navigation options.

parameters.name: scroll
parameters.description: Whether navigation should scroll to the top; defaults to the framework’s navigation behavior.

parameters.name: transitionTypes
parameters.description: Transition type names passed to React’s navigation transition API.

Navigation hooks::useRouter.returns: Returns a router object with push, replace, refresh, back, forward, and prefetch methods.

example.title: Client-side route actions
example.explanation: A Client Component uses the App Router hook to navigate, refresh the current route, and return to the previous history entry.

useCases.title: Event-driven navigation
useCases.scenario: A form or button must navigate after client-side validation or a completed action.

useCases.title: History replacement
useCases.scenario: A search or filter interaction should update the URL without adding many Back-button entries.

useCases.title: Refresh route data
useCases.scenario: The current route needs fresh server-rendered data after a client-side mutation.

useCases.title: Programmatic prefetch
useCases.scenario: A likely next destination should load before the user selects it.

interview.question: What is useRouter and where can it be used?
interview.answer: useRouter is an App Router hook imported from next/navigation and used in Client Components. It exposes imperative methods such as push, replace, refresh, back, forward, and prefetch.
interview.followUp: How would you observe URL changes? Use usePathname and useSearchParams, typically combined in an effect, rather than expecting pathname or query fields on this router.

interview.question: How do push and replace differ?
interview.answer: push performs client-side navigation and adds a history entry. replace performs client-side navigation without adding a new browser-history entry, so Back will not return to the replaced URL.
interview.followUp: When should replace be preferred? Use it when changing the URL should not create a separate history step, such as updating search state during an interaction.

interview.question: What does router.refresh do?
interview.answer: refresh makes a new server request, re-fetches data, and re-renders Server Components. The updated React Server Component payload is merged while unaffected client React state and browser state, such as scroll position, are preserved.
interview.followUp: Does refresh guarantee new data? No; cached or otherwise unchanged fetch results may still be reused, so the server-side caching or revalidation policy also matters.

keyPoints: Use the hook for imperative route changes initiated by client-side events.
router.push navigates to a destination without a full-page browser reload.
router.replace changes the current history entry instead of appending another one.
router.refresh updates the current route from the server while retaining unaffected client and browser state.
router.back follows the browser’s previous history entry.
router.forward moves to the next available history entry.
router.prefetch loads route resources ahead of an eventual navigation.
gotchas: Prefer Link for ordinary navigation; use this hook when navigation must be triggered by client logic.
Do not use the Pages Router import in an App Router component.
Sanitize destinations because injected javascript: URLs can execute in the page context.

Navigation hooks::useRouter back and for.summary: Use the App Router’s `useRouter` hook in a Client Component to traverse existing browser history. Call `router.back()` for the previous entry and `router.forward()` for the next entry.
Navigation hooks::useRouter back and for.explanation: In a Client Component, call `useRouter()` from `next/navigation` to obtain the App Router instance. Its `back()` method moves to the previous browser-history entry, while `forward()` moves to the next one, so navigation follows existing history rather than constructing a new destination.
Navigation hooks::useRouter back and for.returns: `useRouter()` returns a router object; this card uses its `back()` and `forward()` methods to traverse browser history.

example.title: Browser history controls
example.explanation: A Client Component renders controls that move through the browser history stack without specifying a destination URL.

useCases.title: Close a history-backed view
useCases.scenario: A modal or detail view was opened from another route and should close by returning to the prior history entry.

useCases.title: Build history controls
useCases.scenario: A custom navigation toolbar should reproduce browser-style backward and forward movement.

useCases.title: Resume forward navigation
useCases.scenario: An application flow needs to revisit the next browser-history entry after moving backward.

interview.question: What does `router.back()` do?
interview.answer: `router.back()` navigates to the previous route in the browser’s history stack. It is the programmatic equivalent of moving backward through browser history, rather than navigating to an arbitrary URL.
interview.followUp: How would you implement a fallback when there may be no prior entry? The documented method has no fallback parameter, so application code must define and handle that policy separately.

interview.question: What does `router.forward()` do?
interview.answer: `router.forward()` navigates to the next page in the browser’s history stack. It uses the existing forward history entry instead of receiving a destination path.
interview.followUp: What happens after a new navigation replaces the current history branch? The browser’s forward entries may no longer be available, so the control should tolerate having nothing to advance to.

interview.question: How do you use these methods in the App Router?
interview.answer: The hook is imported from `next/navigation` and used inside a Client Component. Calling `useRouter()` provides the router object whose `back()` and `forward()` methods control history navigation.
interview.followUp: Why should a Server Component not call this hook? The documentation limits this hook to Client Components, so server-rendered code should use supported server-side navigation patterns instead.

keyPoints: Import `useRouter` from `next/navigation` when a Client Component needs imperative route control.
Call `router.back()` to move one entry toward the beginning of browser history.
Call `router.forward()` to move one entry toward the end of browser history.
The returned router object exposes these methods for event handlers such as button clicks.
gotchas: Use this hook only in a Client Component; it is not an API for Server Components.
`back()` depends on an earlier history entry; it does not accept a fallback URL.
`forward()` only advances when a forward history entry exists.

Navigation hooks::useRouter hard navigat.explanation: In a Client Component, useRouter exposes imperative navigation methods. Pass only application-controlled paths to push or replace; untrusted values could be interpreted as executable schemes such as javascript: and create an XSS vulnerability.

parameters.name: href
parameters.description: The destination route to navigate to.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional navigation settings, including scroll behavior and transition types.

Navigation hooks::useRouter hard navigat.returns: The useRouter hook returns a router object with imperative navigation methods, including push and replace.

example.title: Navigate to a trusted internal route
example.explanation: The button navigates to a trusted, fixed internal route through the App Router.

useCases.title: Event-driven internal navigation
useCases.scenario: A click handler needs to move a user to a known application route.

useCases.title: Client-side route updates
useCases.scenario: A filter or workflow step should update the route without a full page reload.

useCases.title: Validated conditional navigation
useCases.scenario: A redirect destination comes from application logic and has been checked against allowed paths.

interview.question: What is useRouter used for in the App Router?
interview.answer: useRouter is a Client Component hook for programmatic route changes. Its push method performs client-side navigation and adds a history entry.
interview.followUp: How should a destination derived from user input be handled? Validate it against an allowlist of trusted internal routes before passing it to navigation.

interview.question: Why is unsanitized navigation input dangerous?
interview.answer: Do not pass untrusted or unsanitized URLs to router.push or router.replace. The documentation specifically warns that a javascript: URL can execute in the context of the page and cause XSS.
interview.followUp: What is the safest default for a fixed destination? Keep the path in application code, such as /account, rather than accepting an arbitrary URL.

interview.question: How do push and replace differ, and what safety rule applies to both?
interview.answer: router.push performs client-side navigation to the supplied route and creates a new browser-history entry. router.replace navigates without adding a new entry, but both methods require trusted URL input.
interview.followUp: When no imperative navigation is needed, what should be preferred? Use the Link component instead of calling useRouter.

keyPoints: Use useRouter when a Client Component must trigger navigation from code, such as an event handler.
router.push accepts a route string plus navigation options and performs client-side navigation.
Calling push lets the browser's Back action return to the previous location.
router.replace provides programmatic navigation without the history behavior of push.
Navigation methods must receive trusted destinations because executable URL schemes are a security risk.
gotchas: Never pass user-controlled or otherwise unsanitized URLs directly to router.push or router.replace.
A javascript: URL can execute in the page context, so treating navigation input as harmless text is unsafe.

Observability hooks::useReportWebVitals.summary: Use `useReportWebVitals` in a Client Component to receive Core Web Vitals and send metric data to an analytics endpoint. Include navigation identifiers or URL when attributing measurements across App Router navigations.
