The callback can forward the metric name, measured value, rating, and navigation identifiers or URL to any analytics endpoint; keep the callback reference stable to avoid duplicate reports.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Callback invoked with each available web-vitals metric; the callback can forward the metric to an analytics service.

Observability hooks::useReportWebVitals.returns: No return value is documented; the hook reports metrics through the supplied callback.

example.title: Report Web Vitals
example.explanation: A client component serializes each metric, including navigation context, and sends it to an application analytics endpoint.

useCases.title: Custom performance analytics
useCases.scenario: Send serialized metric objects to a server endpoint for storage and dashboarding.

useCases.title: Soft-navigation attribution
useCases.scenario: Associate delayed soft-navigation measurements with the navigation that produced them.

useCases.title: Performance debugging
useCases.scenario: Inspect metric names and values during development or production diagnostics.

interview.question: What is useReportWebVitals used for?
interview.answer: The hook accepts a callback and calls it with available performance metrics. The callback can send each metric to an analytics service or endpoint.
interview.followUp: What prevents duplicate reports? Keep the callback reference unchanged, because new callback functions can be invoked with metrics already available.

interview.question: Which data identifies a metric and its navigation?
interview.answer: The metric includes fields such as `id`, `name`, and navigation context. `name` identifies the metric, while `navigationId` and `navigationURL` identify the navigation measured.
interview.followUp: Why is navigation context valuable? Soft-navigation metrics can arrive after the browser URL has changed, so the metric's own navigation fields preserve attribution.

interview.question: How is the hook used with the App Router?
interview.answer: Because the hook must run in a Client Component, create a separate component with the `'use client'` directive and import it into the root layout. This limits the client boundary to that component and its imports.
interview.followUp: How should the component be integrated? Keep the Web Vitals component separate and render or import it from the application root layout.

keyPoints: Use the hook to report Core Web Vitals and connect those measurements to an analytics service.
The supplied callback receives metrics that are available when the callback is processed.
The callback argument is a metric object containing several properties for identification and measurement.
`id` distinguishes a metric within the current page load.
Forward serialized metric results to an endpoint of your choice for real-user performance tracking.
`navigationId` associates the measurement with the navigation that produced it.
`navigationURL` records the URL associated with the measured navigation.
gotchas: The hook only works in a Client Component, so place 'use client' before imports in a dedicated component.
Keep the callback function reference stable; changing it can cause duplicate metric reporting.
For soft navigations, use the metric's navigation URL or ID rather than assuming the current browser URL identifies the measured navigation.

Rules and boundaries::Hooks in Client Co.summary: Next.js navigation and browser-dependent hooks must run below a 'use client' boundary. Keep the client-only portion small, and use Suspense around URL-reading hooks when prerendering requires a fallback.
Rules and boundaries::Hooks in Client Co.explanation: In the App Router, navigation hooks such as usePathname, useSearchParams, and useRouter belong in Client Components. Put 'use client' at the top of the module that uses them, then import the hooks from next/navigation; isolate URL-reading code behind Suspense when prerendering requires a fallback.

example.title: Client navigation component
example.explanation: The file-level directive makes this component part of the client module graph, allowing it to call navigation hooks. The pathname is read from the current URL, while the router performs navigation from the button handler.

useCases.title: Read the current pathname
useCases.scenario: Highlight the active route or display the current pathname in a navigation component.

useCases.title: Read query parameters
useCases.scenario: Filter, search, or paginate using values encoded in the URL query string.

useCases.title: Perform programmatic navigation
useCases.scenario: Navigate after a click, form action, or other client-side event that needs imperative control.

interview.question: Where can App Router navigation hooks be used?
interview.answer: Navigation hooks are client-only because they read or change browser URL state. Add 'use client' at the top of the module, then import the required hook from next/navigation.
interview.followUp: How should a prerendered component using useSearchParams be structured? Put the small hook-using component below a Suspense boundary so Next.js can prerender a fallback.

interview.question: What do usePathname and useRouter provide?
interview.answer: usePathname returns the current URL pathname, while useRouter provides imperative methods such as push, replace, refresh, back, and forward. Both are used from Client Components.
interview.followUp: When should Link be chosen instead? Use Link for declarative route navigation unless a specific interaction requires imperative router methods.

interview.question: What is the prerendering consequence of useSearchParams?
interview.answer: useSearchParams reads the current URL query string and is unavailable in Server Components. On a prerendered route, it can cause the client tree up to the nearest Suspense boundary to be client-rendered.
interview.followUp: How can the client-rendered area be minimized? Extract the hook call into a small Client Component and keep the Suspense boundary close to it.

keyPoints: Declare the client boundary before imports in the module that contains browser-dependent or interactive code.
The directive separates the server and client dependency graphs; imports below it participate in the client side of that boundary.
Use usePathname when a client component needs the current route pathname.
Use useRouter for imperative route changes from client-side interactions.
Using a Client Component for navigation state is part of the intended Server Components architecture, not automatically a performance failure.
gotchas: Prefer Link for ordinary navigation; reserve useRouter for cases that specifically need programmatic control.

Rules and boundaries::Next.js hook migra.sourceTitle: How to migrate from Pages to the App Router
Rules and boundaries::Next.js hook migra.summary: When moving a screen into the App Router, replace next/router usage with hooks from next/navigation. Separate navigation, pathname, search-parameter, and dynamic-parameter concerns, and use these hooks only in Client Components.
Rules and boundaries::Next.js hook migra.explanation: When a screen moves into the App Router, replace the Pages Router import with hooks from next/navigation. Use useRouter for programmatic navigation, and usePathname, useSearchParams, or useParams for values formerly obtained from router.pathname or router.query. These hooks belong in Client Components; combine pathname and search parameters when reacting to route changes.
Rules and boundaries::Next.js hook migra.syntax: import { useRouter, usePathname, useSearchParams, useParams } from "next/navigation"
Rules and boundaries::Next.js hook migra.returns: The hooks return routing capabilities or route state: useRouter returns the App Router router object; usePathname returns the current pathname; useSearchParams returns URL search parameters; useParams returns dynamic route parameters.

example.title: App Router navigation hooks
example.explanation: A Client Component uses separate App Router hooks for navigation, the current pathname, and URL search parameters.

useCases.title: Programmatic navigation
useCases.scenario: A migrated client-side screen needs to redirect, replace the current URL, refresh route data, or navigate backward.

useCases.title: Path-based UI
useCases.scenario: A component must build UI from the current path or react when the path changes.

useCases.title: Search-parameter state
useCases.scenario: A search, filter, or pagination control reads or updates URL query-string values.

useCases.title: Dynamic route parameters
useCases.scenario: A migrated route renders content based on dynamic segments such as an identifier or slug.

interview.question: How does useRouter differ after moving a screen to the App Router?
interview.answer: Import useRouter from next/navigation in an App Router screen, not next/router. The App Router hook is for programmatic route changes inside Client Components.
interview.followUp: How do you preserve a component during an incremental migration? Use next/compat/router while it still runs in both routers, then switch to next/navigation after it is App Router-only.

interview.question: How do you replace router.pathname and router.query?
interview.answer: The App Router useRouter no longer exposes pathname or query. Read the pathname with usePathname, URL search parameters with useSearchParams, and dynamic segments with useParams.
interview.followUp: How would you detect navigation changes without router.events? Combine usePathname and useSearchParams, typically in an effect whose dependencies include those values.

interview.question: Where can the new navigation hooks be used?
interview.answer: These migration hooks are Client Component hooks, so the component using them must be marked as a Client Component. Server Components cannot call them.
interview.followUp: What should a shared component use while it supports both routers? Use the compatibility router from next/compat/router and handle its possibly unavailable router state during the transition.

keyPoints: For App Router screens, use the navigation hooks from next/navigation: useRouter, usePathname, and useSearchParams.
A screen previously using the Pages Router useRouter needs its routing-hook imports and usage migrated when placed under app.
Replace reads of router.pathname with the standalone usePathname hook.
Split former router.query usage between useSearchParams for search parameters and useParams for dynamic route parameters.
Use pathname and search-parameter hooks together when a component needs to respond to route changes.
gotchas: The App Router navigation hooks cannot be used from Server Components; place them in a Client Component.
Do not read pathname from the new router object; call usePathname instead.
Do not expect a query object; use useSearchParams for query-string values and useParams for dynamic route parameters.
Pages Router router.events has no direct equivalent; use usePathname and useSearchParams together to observe page changes.

URL hooks::URL hooks and Suspense.summary: On a prerendered route, isolate useSearchParams in a small Client Component wrapped by Suspense. This preserves prerendering for the surrounding route while the query-dependent subtree renders on the client.
URL hooks::URL hooks and Suspense.explanation: On a prerendered App Router route, useSearchParams reads request-time query data, so Next.js client-renders the tree up to the nearest Suspense boundary. Put the hook in a small Client Component and wrap it with Suspense to preserve prerendering for the rest of the route and provide fallback HTML until the query value is available.
URL hooks::URL hooks and Suspense.returns: A read-only URLSearchParams-like object representing the current URL query parameters.

example.title: Isolate query-state reading
example.explanation: The hook is kept in a small Client Component, while Suspense lets the surrounding route remain in the prerendered shell.

useCases.title: Search and filtering
useCases.scenario: A statically generated page contains a search box whose results depend on the q query parameter.

useCases.title: URL-driven controls
useCases.scenario: A dashboard has a client-side sorting or pagination control encoded in the URL.

useCases.title: Preserve a static shell
useCases.scenario: A mostly static page includes one widget that reads request-time query state.

interview.question: Why does useSearchParams need Suspense on a prerendered route?
interview.answer: useSearchParams is a Client Component hook for reading the current URL query string. On a prerendered route, query data is unavailable during prerendering, so the affected tree must be handled by Suspense.
interview.followUp: How do you minimize the client-rendered area? Move the hook into the smallest child Client Component and place the boundary around that child.

interview.question: What does the nearest Suspense boundary control?
interview.answer: The closest Suspense boundary determines how much of the Client Component tree is client-rendered. A boundary around the query reader allows components above it to remain prerendered and included in the initial HTML.
interview.followUp: What is the consequence of putting the boundary too high? More of the route becomes client-rendered, reducing the prerendered static shell.

interview.question: Why might a missing boundary go unnoticed during development?
interview.answer: During development, routes render on demand, so the hook may appear to work without Suspense. A production build exposes the requirement for static pages and can fail with the missing-boundary error.
interview.followUp: How should the implementation be validated? Run a production build rather than relying only on development behavior.

keyPoints: On a prerendered route, the hook makes the Client Component tree up to the nearest Suspense boundary render on the client.
Suspense splits the route into a prerendered portion and a query-dependent client-rendered portion.
Place the boundary directly around the Client Component that reads the query.
Components above the boundary can still be prerendered and delivered in the initial HTML.
gotchas: Development can hide the problem because on-demand rendering may not suspend; verify with a production build.
A statically generated page fails its production build when the Client Component using the hook is outside Suspense.
Omitting the boundary can trigger a full client-rendering bailout instead of limiting client rendering to the query-dependent subtree.

URL hooks::useParams.summary: useParams reads dynamic parameters from the active URL in a Next.js App Router Client Component. It returns an object keyed by dynamic segment name, with string or string-array values depending on the segment type.
URL hooks::useParams.explanation: Import this Client Component hook from next/navigation and call it without arguments. It returns an object whose keys are active dynamic segment names; each value is a string for a single segment or a string array for a catch-all segment. A route without dynamic segments produces an empty object.
URL hooks::useParams.returns: An object containing the active route's dynamic parameters. Each key is a segment name, and each value is a string or string array based on the segment type; routes without dynamic parameters return an empty object.

example.title: Read a dynamic segment
example.explanation: In a Client Component under app/blog/[slug], the hook reads the active slug segment from the URL.

useCases.title: Read a resource identifier
useCases.scenario: A page or nested component needs the [slug] value to load or label the current resource.

useCases.title: Use multiple dynamic segments
useCases.scenario: A component is rendered below a [category]/[item] route and needs both active segment values.

useCases.title: Handle catch-all paths
useCases.scenario: A catch-all route such as [...parts] needs its matched path pieces for navigation or rendering.

interview.question: What does useParams do?
interview.answer: useParams reads dynamic route segments from the active URL. It takes no arguments and returns an object mapping each active segment name to its value.
interview.followUp: How does a catch-all segment differ? Its mapped value is an array of strings rather than one string.

interview.question: How do you use useParams in the App Router?
interview.answer: It is imported from next/navigation and used in a Client Component. A route such as app/blog/[slug] exposes a slug property on the returned object.
interview.followUp: What must change for app/blog/[...slug]? The slug property should be handled as a string array.

interview.question: What does useParams return, and what does it not return?
interview.answer: The hook returns only dynamic route parameters, not query-string parameters. A route with no dynamic parameters returns an empty object.
interview.followUp: Which API should be considered for query-string values? Use the separate useSearchParams hook for the URL query string.

keyPoints: Call the hook with no arguments.
Returned object keys correspond to dynamic segments present in the active route.
A key such as slug maps to the URL value matched by [slug].
The segment syntax determines whether the result is a string or an array of strings.
Static routes yield {} rather than a parameter value.
It reads values from the currently active URL rather than from a manually supplied pathname.
gotchas: The component using the hook must be a Client Component, so include 'use client' at the top of its file.
Catch-all and optional catch-all segments return arrays, while ordinary dynamic segments return strings; type the result accordingly.
Do not expect a value when the active route has no dynamic segment.

URL hooks::useParams with catch-all rout.summary: Use `useParams` in an App Router Client Component to read dynamic values from the current URL. Single segments return strings, while catch-all and optional catch-all segments return string arrays.
URL hooks::useParams with catch-all rout.explanation: In an App Router Client Component, call `useParams` to obtain the dynamic segments matched by the current URL. A normal dynamic segment produces a string, while catch-all and optional catch-all segments produce string arrays; an optional catch-all route can also omit the property when its segment is absent.

parameters.name: none
parameters.description: `useParams` takes no arguments.

URL hooks::useParams with catch-all rout.returns: An object containing the current route's filled dynamic parameters. Each active dynamic segment becomes a property whose value is a string or an array of strings; a route with no dynamic parameters returns an empty object.

example.explanation: This client component reads the optional catch-all `slug` value, joins its URL segments for display, and uses `home` when `/docs` has no captured segments.

useCases.title: Read a variable-depth path

useCases.title: Display the current dynamic location

interview.question: What does `useParams` do in the App Router?
interview.answer: `useParams` is a Client Component hook that reads dynamic parameters from the current URL. It takes no arguments and returns an object whose properties correspond to active dynamic segments.
interview.followUp: What type does a catch-all value have? A catch-all or optional catch-all segment supplies an array of strings rather than one string.

interview.question: How are catch-all route parameters represented?
interview.answer: A segment written as `[...slug]` captures all subsequent URL segments, so its value is a string array. For example, `/shop/a/b` supplies `slug: ["a", "b"]`.
interview.followUp: How does the optional form differ? `[[...slug]]` also matches the parent path, such as `/shop`, when no slug segments exist.

interview.question: How does the returned object map to route segments?
interview.answer: `useParams` returns an object with one property for each active dynamic segment. The property name comes from the segment name, and its value is a string or string array based on the segment type.
interview.followUp: What happens if a route has no dynamic parameters? The hook returns an empty object.

keyPoints: Import `useParams` from `next/navigation` and call it inside a Client Component to read the current route's dynamic values.
A single bracket segment such as `[id]` is a string; catch-all forms use arrays of strings.
Use `[...slug]` when the route must capture one or more remaining path segments.
Use `[[...slug]]` when the parent route should match even without any captured trailing segments.
A catch-all route consumes multiple path levels, not just the next single segment.
The optional variant matches both the base path and deeper paths; the required catch-all variant does not match the base path alone.
gotchas: Do not expect query-string values or unrelated route data; a route without dynamic segments yields an empty object.
With Cache Components, unresolved request-time parameters can suspend, so provide a Suspense boundary when the documentation's conditions require it.

URL hooks::usePathname.summary: usePathname reads the current URL pathname from a Next.js Client Component. It takes no arguments and returns the pathname string without query parameters.
URL hooks::usePathname.explanation: Import the hook from next/navigation inside a Client Component, call it without arguments, and use the returned pathname in rendered UI. The component is included in the initial HTML, then remains available in the client bundle and re-renders when navigation changes the current route.
URL hooks::usePathname.returns: A string containing the current URL pathname.

example.title: Display the current pathname
example.explanation: This Client Component reads the pathname and displays it; query-string parameters are not included.

useCases.title: Highlight the active link
useCases.scenario: A navigation menu compares the current pathname with each link's href to mark the active route.

useCases.title: Build breadcrumbs
useCases.scenario: A breadcrumb component splits the pathname into segments to display route context.

useCases.title: React to route changes
useCases.scenario: An effect depends on pathname to perform client-side work after navigation changes the route.

interview.question: What does usePathname return, and where can it be used?
interview.answer: usePathname is a Client Component hook from next/navigation. It returns the current URL pathname as a string, without the query string.
interview.followUp: How can a component react to route changes? Include the pathname in a dependency array, optionally alongside useSearchParams, for an effect that should run after navigation.

interview.question: What is the signature of usePathname?
interview.answer: The hook takes no parameters. A call such as usePathname() returns the current pathname, such as /dashboard or /blog/hello-world.
interview.followUp: What value corresponds to a URL like /dashboard?v=2? The returned pathname is /dashboard because the query string is excluded.

interview.question: Why does usePathname require a Client Component?
interview.answer: The component using the hook must be a Client Component, so the file needs the 'use client' directive. Client Components using it are rendered into initial HTML and then re-render from client state during navigation.
interview.followUp: Why not read the pathname directly in a Server Component? The documented hook is intentionally client-only; use a Client Component boundary for pathname-dependent UI.

keyPoints: Use this hook when client-side UI needs to know which route is currently active.
Add the 'use client' directive to the component file before importing and calling the hook.
Call it directly as usePathname(); there is no options object or argument.
The result is a pathname string rather than the complete URL.
After the initial client bundle is downloaded, navigation updates the component through re-rendering instead of fetching it again.
For a URL containing a query string, the returned value contains only the path portion.

URL hooks::usePathname with rewrites.summary: Use usePathname in a Client Component to read the current pathname. With rewrites, isolate pathname-dependent UI and defer its update until after mount so server and browser markup remain consistent.
URL hooks::usePathname with rewrites.explanation: usePathname is a Client Component hook that returns the current URL pathname. With a statically prerendered page reached through a rewrite, the server can render using the source pathname while the browser uses the rewritten pathname, so isolate pathname-dependent UI and update it after mount.
URL hooks::usePathname with rewrites.returns: `usePathname` returns a string of the current URL's pathname.

example.title: Defer rewritten pathname UI until mount
example.explanation: Reads the pathname only after mounting, leaving a stable server-rendered fallback when a rewrite makes the browser pathname differ from the statically generated source path.

useCases.title: Rewrite-aware active navigation
useCases.scenario: A navigation component highlights the current route after a rewrite.

useCases.title: Pathname-dependent status UI
useCases.scenario: A small client widget displays the browser-visible path without destabilizing the page's server HTML.

interview.question: What does usePathname return, and where can it be used?
interview.answer: usePathname is a Client Component hook that returns the current URL pathname as a string. It lets client-rendered UI respond to pathname changes.
interview.followUp: Why should a Server Component not read it directly? The documented pattern places URL-dependent behavior in a Client Component, preserving server-component layout state across navigations.

interview.question: Why can rewrites cause hydration mismatches with usePathname?
interview.answer: With static prerendering and a rewrite, the server generates HTML for the source pathname, while the browser may show the rewritten pathname. Rendering pathname-dependent UI immediately can therefore cause a hydration mismatch.
interview.followUp: What is the safest UI design? Keep the pathname-dependent portion small and isolated rather than making the entire page depend on the client-only value.

interview.question: How should pathname-dependent UI be implemented when rewrites are configured?
interview.answer: Render a stable fallback during the server render, then read or apply the pathname after the component mounts. This keeps the initial markup consistent before the browser-specific pathname is available.
interview.followUp: What user-visible trade-off remains? The fallback may flash briefly; the documentation points to techniques for preventing that flash before hydration.

keyPoints: Call usePathname only from a Client Component to obtain the current URL pathname.
For a prerendered route, the server initially creates HTML based on the pathname before rewriting.
After a rewrite, the browser-visible pathname can differ from the source pathname used for generated HTML.
Limit pathname-dependent rendering to a small isolated client region.
Use server-stable fallback markup, then replace it with pathname-dependent content after mounting.
The hook's return value is a pathname string, not the query string or hash.
gotchas: A statically prerendered page using rewrites can produce different server and browser pathnames, causing hydration errors.
Deferring the pathname read avoids the mismatch but can briefly display the fallback.

URL hooks::useSearchParams.summary: useSearchParams is a Client Component hook for reading the current URL query string. It returns a read-only URLSearchParams interface.
URL hooks::useSearchParams.explanation: Import useSearchParams from next/navigation inside a Client Component, then call it to obtain a read-only URLSearchParams-like object for the current URL. Use its reading methods, such as get(), to inspect query values; the hook updates when navigation changes the URL.
URL hooks::useSearchParams.returns: A read-only URLSearchParams interface for the current query string.

example.title: Read a query parameter
example.explanation: Reads the current query parameter in a Client Component and renders a fallback when it is absent.

useCases.title: Client-side filtering
useCases.scenario: A Client Component filters or searches data already loaded through props using values from the URL.

useCases.title: Search and pagination state
useCases.scenario: A search or pagination control reads query values to render the current UI state.

useCases.title: URL-synchronized UI
useCases.scenario: A navigation-driven Client Component needs the latest query parameters after URL changes.

interview.question: What does useSearchParams return, and can you mutate it?
interview.answer: useSearchParams is a Client Component hook from next/navigation. It returns a read-only URLSearchParams interface, so it is intended for reading the current query string rather than mutating it.
interview.followUp: How would you change the query string? Create a separate URLSearchParams instance from searchParams.toString(), modify that instance, and navigate with the desired URL.

interview.question: How do you read a query parameter with this hook?
interview.answer: The hook takes no arguments. Its returned interface provides URLSearchParams reading utilities, including get(), which returns the first value associated with a parameter.
interview.followUp: How can repeated values be handled? Use the corresponding URLSearchParams utilities, such as getAll(), when all values for a name are needed.

interview.question: Why is useSearchParams restricted to Client Components?
interview.answer: It is unavailable in Server Components because server rendering and partial rendering could otherwise expose stale query values. To read search parameters on the server, use the Page searchParams prop instead.
interview.followUp: When is this hook preferable? Use it when the parameter is needed only in the client, such as filtering data already provided through props.

keyPoints: It reads the query string for the current URL from a Client Component.
The returned object exposes URLSearchParams-style access without allowing direct mutation.
Call the hook without passing arguments.
Use get() when you need the first value for a named query parameter.
gotchas: The hook is client-only and must not be called from a Server Component.
Projects that still contain a /pages directory should handle the possible null return type.

URL hooks::useSearchParams values.summary: Read the current URL query string in a Client Component. Use get for one value, getAll for repeated values, and keep the returned object read-only.
URL hooks::useSearchParams values.explanation: In a Client Component, call useSearchParams to obtain a read-only URLSearchParams-like object for the current URL. Use get for the first matching value, getAll for repeated values, and has or other URLSearchParams read methods as needed; create a separate URLSearchParams instance if values must be changed.
URL hooks::useSearchParams values.returns: A read-only URLSearchParams interface representing the current URL's query string.

example.title: Read query values in a Client Component
example.explanation: Reads one value, all repeated values, and a decoded value from the current query string without changing the read-only object.

useCases.title: Client-side filtering
useCases.scenario: A client-rendered search or filter control needs the current query value to display matching UI.

useCases.title: Repeated query keys
useCases.scenario: A URL permits the same key more than once, such as tag=one&tag=two.

useCases.title: Optional query settings
useCases.scenario: A component needs an optional query setting, such as a selected tab or redirect target.

interview.question: What does useSearchParams return?
interview.answer: useSearchParams is a Client Component hook from next/navigation. It reads the current URL query string and returns a read-only URLSearchParams interface.
interview.followUp: How would you update a query value? Copy searchParams with new URLSearchParams(searchParams.toString()), mutate the copy, then navigate with the updated query string.

interview.question: How do you read repeated and missing query values?
interview.answer: get('key') returns the first value for that key, or null when the key is absent. For a query such as a=1&a=2, use getAll('a') to retrieve every value.
interview.followUp: What should code do when a parameter is optional? Check for null or provide an explicit fallback before rendering or using the value.

interview.question: Why must useSearchParams run in a Client Component?
interview.answer: The hook is unavailable in Server Components because it could expose stale values during partial rendering. Use the page's searchParams prop for server-side page behavior, or move client-only reading into a Client Component.
interview.followUp: When is the page prop preferable? Use it when search parameters must load data for the page; use this hook for client-only use such as filtering already-loaded data.

keyPoints: Import it from next/navigation and call it inside a Client Component to read the current URL's query string.
The returned object follows URLSearchParams reading behavior but is intentionally read-only.
Use get(name) when only the first matching query value is relevant.
Use getAll(name) when the same query key can occur multiple times.
A missing key produces null from get, so optional values need a null check or fallback.
The hook exposes URLSearchParams utility methods for reading query values, including get.
gotchas: Only call this hook from a Client Component; Server Components cannot use it.
Do not call mutation methods such as set, append, or delete on the returned object; copy it first if mutation is required.
get returns only the first occurrence, so repeated keys require getAll.
The hook has no configuration argument; select the query key with URLSearchParams methods instead.
